title: Elul: the king in the field
hookLine: Shneur Zalman's parable: in Elul the king walks out to meet people in the fields
carry: the king is in the field

lines: TO SEE A KING, YOU EARNED IT.
ONCE A YEAR, HE RIDES OUT.
cards: To see a king in the old world, you had to earn it. You traveled to the capital and waited outside the palace. Guards checked who you were.
Officials decided whether you mattered enough. If you got in at all, you bowed, said your piece fast, and were walked out.
Now suppose that once a year the king leaves the palace and rides out into the countryside, and anyone working in the fields can walk right up to him.

teach.b: This parable comes from Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi, the founder of Chabad Hasidism. He told it about Elul, the last month of the Jewish year, just before Rosh Hashanah.
Before a king enters his city, he says, the people go out to meet him in the field.

teach.h: ANYONE MAY APPROACH IN THE FIELD.
teach.b: There anyone may approach, and he receives them all with a pleasant face, a shining countenance. Farmers in their work clothes, no appointment.
Then he enters the city, and they follow him to the palace, where only invited guests get in.

teach.h: THE PALACE IS THE DAYS OF AWE.
teach.b: The palace is Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur: the grand, awesome days, the full congregation, the long services. The field is Elul, the quiet month before, when the closeness is easy and anyone can come as they are.
There's an old way of finding Elul in a verse, too. The Song of Songs says: "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine."
In Hebrew, ani l'dodi v'dodi li. The first letters of those four words, aleph, lamed, vav, lamed, spell Elul, so the month is read as a love song between God and the people.
During Elul many communities add Psalm 27 to their daily prayers, a psalm about seeking God's face and hoping to dwell in God's house. The month before judgment could be a month of dread.
Shneur Zalman makes it a month of closeness.

teach.h: THE KING IS IN THE FIELD.
teach.b: The king is out in the field, and the field is where you already are.

how: During Elul many Jews take stock of the past year, add Psalm 27 to daily prayer, give more charity and prepare for Rosh Hashanah; in Chabad and other Hasidic communities Shneur Zalman's parable of the king in the field is often retold.

o: the last month of the Jewish year, before Rosh Hashanah
the first month of spring, when Passover falls
the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur

games.q: inside the king in the field — tap the pairs.

s: the parable says the month before judgment is the hardest time to approach God
it says the opposite: in Elul the king is in the field, and anyone may come.
the first letters of 'I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine' spell Elul in Hebrew
ani l'dodi v'dodi li: aleph, lamed, vav, lamed.
Elul is the last month of the Jewish year
it comes just before Rosh Hashanah.

games.q: you're a farmer in the parable. the king rides out past your field, smiling. you're in your work clothes. what do you do?
o: walk up to him as you are.
wait for an invitation to the palace.
games.why: in the field, anyone may approach, and he receives them all with a pleasant face. that's Elul.

practice: Step outside if you can, or go to a window, and look at what's actually there: the street, a tree, the sky, a parked car, without dressing it up. This is the field.
If you pray, picture the king of the parable out here in the ordinary, receiving you as you are; if not, let yourself meet the day without preparing for it first.

wordCard.voice: Elul. The last month of the Jewish year, before Rosh Hashanah. The month, Shneur Zalman taught, when the king is in the field.
